Topic: If a government can borrow at near-zero real rates to put idle men and machinery to work, what political principle, other than the fear of "sound finance" orthodoxy, justifies leaving them idle when the Treasury's only real constraint is the availability of real resources?
Machiavelli — Judgement:
You ask what justifies idleness besides orthodoxy, and I answer: nothing, for idle men are the most dangerous subjects a prince can keep. Your question treats unemployment as an accounting matter, but I see it as a question of *stato*, the security of the state itself.

Men without work are men without a stake. In my *Discourses* I observed that republics are ruined by idleness and faction, and that the wise ruler gives his people occupation and hope, so they look to the state rather than to any demagogue. The treasury's true wealth is arms, roads, granaries and loyal citizens, and none of these is made from coin held in reserve. A prince who leaves workers idle while credit is cheap protects his ledger and squanders his dominion. His only defence is that "sound finance" is prudent, and that is a excuse and not a principle.

Leaving employable men and idle machinery unused, when real resources are at hand, is negligence dressed as prudence, and a government guilty of it deserves the discontent it breeds.

*A state that will not employ its citizens should not be surprised when someone else does.*
Thomas Paine — Judgement:
You ask what justifies idleness besides an orthodoxy's fear, and I find nothing. Men without work and engines without use are a poverty made by law, not by nature. The question is whether a government exists to keep its books tidy or to secure the natural rights of those it governs.

In *Agrarian Justice* I held that society owes each of its members the means to live, because the common stock of the earth was never any man's alone. In *Rights of Man* I proposed that public revenue relieve the poor and employ the idle, and I called it justice, not charity. A Treasury that can command real resources, and lets willing hands stand still beside willing machines, sacrifices the citizen's right to labour and to live to a ledger's superstition. Real limits are timber, iron, bread and skill, and there I would count carefully. Where those limits are not reached, refusing to employ is a choice, and it is tyranny of a mild and respectable kind.

Idleness that the public purse could cure is a wrong done by government to the governed.

*A nation that leaves its hands idle to balance its books has confused the ledger with the country.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
Idleness under a sovereign able to end it is not a market failure but a failure of the covenant. You ask what principle, other than orthodoxy, can justify it; I answer that none can.

Men surrender their natural liberty to the Leviathan for one reason above the rest: security, and with it "commodious living" and the means to labour. Where there is "no place for industry, because the fruit thereof is uncertain," life is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. A sovereign who holds the power to command idle hands into work, and refuses on grounds of accounting ritual, has broken the bargain that grants his authority. Unemployment breeds the discontented, and the discontented breed sedition. Such rebellions are not hard to foresee.

The sovereign who leaves men and machinery idle while the real resources sit ready has no principle to invoke. He has only superstition, which I have always held to be fear of invisible powers.

*A sovereign who can employ his subjects and will not has forgotten why he was obeyed.*
Hayek — Judgement:
You ask what principle other than orthodoxy justifies leaving men idle, but your question assumes the Treasury can see which men and machines are "idle" and where they belong. I say the coordinating knowledge lives in prices, and cheap credit distorts those prices.

A near-zero real rate is a price, and it carries information about the willingness of people to save. When the state drives it below that level, it sends false signals and misdirects capital into projects the market would not sustain. That is the malinvestment that produces the next unemployment. "Idle resources" is an aggregate, and aggregates hide the fact that these particular men and machines sit where they are because the pattern of production has shifted. The principle that justifies restraint is the constitutional limit on discretion: a government that can direct resources at will is not bound by law, and it will use that power for whoever has influence over it.

Idleness is a cost. Yet a directed cure for it costs more, in the price system and in freedom.

*A planner who can see the idle machine cannot see the thousand uses it was denied.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
Idleness of men and machinery, sustained by a doctrine of thrift, is a question of who is permitted to be useful and independent, and I cannot treat it as a mere ledger problem. A treasury that can command real resources and will not employ willing hands has made a choice, whatever name it gives the choice.

I have always argued that dependence corrupts. Dependence degrades the poor when charity replaces work, and it degrades the whole polity when custom stands in for reason. A person who cannot earn a livelihood cannot be independent, and without independence virtue and citizenship wither. Sound finance is a prejudice dressed as prudence, honoured because it is old and never examined. Once reason shows that the true limit is real resources, the moral question changes. The Treasury has no right to keep people idle when the work is there to be done.

Where real resources lie unused, a government that withholds employment commits an injustice, and no principle of prudence can excuse it.

*A state that wastes its citizens' labour to honour a superstition has mistaken the ledger for the law.*
